body.heading: Specific beats grand
paragraphs: "You're great" is pleasant and forgettable. "The way you calmed that meeting down when everyone was talking over each other — that took real skill" is a compliment someone carries home with them. The difference is specificity: a genuine compliment notices something real, names it, and says why it mattered.

Specific compliments work because they cannot be faked. Anyone can say "nice job"; only someone who was actually paying attention can say what, exactly, was good about it. That attention is the compliment, as much as the words.

body.heading: How to give one that lands
paragraphs: Start with what you saw, not what you think of the person. "You explained that so clearly that I finally understood it" lands better than "You're so smart." Keep it short — one honest sentence beats a paragraph of praise — and say it soon, while the moment is still warm.

And then stop. Don't soften it with a joke or take it back with a "but". A compliment given plainly and left to stand is a small gift; a compliment that apologises for itself isn't one at all. Try one today: pick something specific, say it simply, and watch the other person's face change.
